title: Online Safety and Cybersecurity Basics
summary: Learn to protect your accounts, money and devices, spot scams, and respond calmly when something goes wrong.
audience: Secondary and university students, and anyone using a phone or computer

body.p: Your passwords are the keys to your email, school portal, social media and sometimes your money. Most account break-ins do not happen because a clever hacker guessed a password. They happen because a password was short, easy to guess, reused on many sites, or handed over to a fake page. A good password habit removes most of that risk.

list: Length matters more than tricks. A passphrase of four or more unrelated words, such as 'orange-river-kettle-moon', is far stronger and easier to remember than 'P@ssw0rd1'.
Never use your name, birth date, phone number, football club or 'password123'. These are the first things a guesser tries.
Use a different password for every important account. If one site leaks its passwords, criminals try the same email and password on other sites.
Do not share passwords with friends, even a boyfriend or girlfriend. Friendships change; passwords stay valid until you change them.

body.p: Nobody can remember 40 different strong passwords. A password manager is an app that stores them in an encrypted vault, protected by one strong master passphrase, and fills them in for you. Your phone or browser may already include one. Make the master passphrase long, unique, and never used anywhere else. If you do not want a manager, a small notebook kept at home is better than reusing one password everywhere, as long as you do not carry it around or photograph it.

Two-step verification (also called two-factor authentication or 2FA) asks for something extra after your password, such as a code from an authenticator app or a prompt on your phone. Even if someone steals your password, they cannot get in without the second step. Codes from an authenticator app are safer than codes sent by SMS, because SMS can be attacked by SIM swapping (covered later in this course). Turn it on first for your main email, because email can reset all your other accounts.

steps: Open your email account's security settings.
Switch on two-step verification and choose an authenticator app if offered.
Save the backup codes somewhere safe and offline, such as written on paper at home.
Repeat for social media, your school portal and any app that holds money.

body.p: Worked example: Kofi uses 'kofi2007' for email, Instagram and his university portal. A small shopping site he once joined is hacked and leaks that password. Within hours, someone tries it on his email and succeeds. If Kofi had used a different passphrase for each account and turned on two-step verification, the leaked password would have been useless.

body.tip: Never tell anyone a verification code, even someone who says they are from the company. Real staff never need it.

body.p: Phishing is when a criminal pretends to be someone you trust to trick you into giving away a password, a code, a PIN or money. It arrives by email, by SMS (smishing), by phone call (vishing) and by WhatsApp or social media messages. The messages change, but the tricks stay the same: they create urgency, fear or excitement so that you act before you think.

list: Urgency or threats: 'Your account will be closed in 24 hours' or 'Your SIM will be blocked today'.
Too good to be true: a prize you did not enter, a free laptop, a visa guaranteed for a fee.
A request for a PIN, password or one-time code. Banks, mobile-money providers and schools do not ask for these.
A link that does not match the real website, or a sender address that is slightly wrong, such as an extra letter or a free email address pretending to be an organisation.
Poor spelling is common, but good spelling does not prove a message is real.

body.p: Fake scholarships often say you have won an award, then ask for a 'processing fee', 'insurance fee' or your bank details. Real scholarships do not charge you to receive money. Fake job offers promise high pay for little work, ask you to pay for training, a uniform or 'registration', or send you a cheque and ask you to return part of it. If an offer asks you to pay first, treat it as a scam. Also be careful with 'investment' schemes that promise to double your money, and with friends' accounts that suddenly ask for urgent money; the friend may have been hacked.

body.h: What to do when a message arrives

steps: Stop. Do not click, reply or call the number in the message.
Ask: who is this really from, and what do they want me to do?
Check independently. Open the official website by typing its address yourself, or call the number printed on your bank card or in the official app.
If it is a friend asking for money, phone them on their normal number to confirm.
Report and delete the message. Block the sender.

body.p: Worked example: Ngozi gets an SMS: 'Congratulations! You have been selected for an overseas scholarship. Pay a 15,000 processing fee to secure your place.' She did not apply for it, it asks for money first, and it uses pressure. She does not pay. She searches the official website of the real scholarship programme, finds a warning about this exact scam, and forwards the message to her school counsellor.

body.tip: Pause for one minute before acting on any message about money, a prize or a locked account. Scammers rely on speed.

lessons.title: Public Wi-Fi, app permissions, privacy and updates

body.p: Your phone holds your photos, messages, contacts and banking apps. Looking after the device and the networks it connects to is as important as having good passwords.

Free Wi-Fi in cafes, airports, campuses and bus stations is convenient but you do not control it. Someone could set up a fake network with a believable name, or watch what unprotected traffic passes through. Safer habits: prefer your mobile data for banking, mobile money and anything with passwords; if you must use public Wi-Fi, only visit sites that show a padlock and 'https', do not log in to sensitive accounts, turn off automatic connection to open networks, and log out and 'forget' the network afterwards. If a Wi-Fi network asks for your PIN or a bank card number, leave.

When an app asks for access to your camera, microphone, contacts, location or photos, ask whether it needs this to do its job. A torch app has no need for your contacts. A map app needs location, but perhaps only while you are using it. Download apps only from your phone's official app store, read recent reviews, and be wary of 'free' versions of paid apps sent over WhatsApp, because they often hide malware. You can review and remove permissions in your phone settings at any time.

list: Set social media accounts to private if you can, so only approved friends see your posts.
Do not post your home address, school timetable, travel plans, ID documents, exam admission slips or boarding passes.
Check who can tag you or see your phone number.
Remember that screenshots exist. Anything you send can be shared by the receiver.

body.p: Updates fix security holes that criminals know about. Switch on automatic updates for your phone and apps. Back up your important files, such as coursework and photos, to a cloud service and, if possible, a second place such as a memory card kept at home. A good rule is three copies: the original, one backup, and one stored elsewhere. Test by opening a backup file occasionally.

Worked example: Efua loses her phone on a bus, with her final-year project on it. Because backup was switched on, she logs in on a friend's phone, recovers the files, and uses her account's 'find my device' feature to lock the lost phone.

body.tip: Set a screen lock with a PIN, fingerprint or pattern that is not your birthday, and keep it private.

body.p: Mobile money and banking apps are used by millions of people across Africa and beyond, and so they attract criminals. Most losses come from tricking the owner, not from breaking the technology. A few firm rules protect you.

list: Never share your PIN with anyone: not a friend, an agent, or a caller from the 'customer care' line. Real staff do not ask for it.
Never share one-time codes sent to you. A code is a key; whoever holds it can act as you.

Check the name and number on the confirmation screen before you send money. Wrong-number requests, such as 'I sent money to you by mistake, please return it', are a common trick. Check your real balance and transaction history before you reverse anything, and contact the provider.
Use only official apps and official short codes from your provider's website.
Keep your PIN different from your phone lock and do not use your birth year.

body.p: In a SIM swap, a criminal convinces your mobile network, or a dishonest insider, to move your phone number to a new SIM card they hold. Calls and SMS codes then go to them, and they can try to reset your passwords and empty accounts that use SMS codes. They often prepare by collecting your name, date of birth and ID details from social media or from phishing.

steps: Warning sign: your phone suddenly has no signal for a long time, although others nearby have signal, and you get no calls or texts.
Use another phone or Wi-Fi to contact your network provider immediately and ask them to block the swap and restore your number.
Contact your bank and mobile-money provider to freeze or protect your accounts.
Change passwords for email and key accounts, starting with email, from a safe device.
Report to the police if money was taken, and keep reference numbers.

body.p: Worked example: Musa gets a call from someone claiming to be from his mobile-money provider. They say his account is 'being upgraded' and ask for the code just sent to his phone. Musa hangs up, because the provider would never ask for it. He calls the official customer line from the provider's website and is told the call was fake. Reducing what strangers can learn about you, such as ID photos and birth dates, makes SIM swap harder.

body.tip: Where possible, use an authenticator app instead of SMS codes for important accounts, so a swapped SIM gives less access.

lessons.title: If your account is hacked, and recovering safely

body.p: Even careful people get hacked. What matters is how quickly and calmly you respond. The faster you act, the less damage is done.

body.h: Signs your account may be compromised

list: Messages or posts you did not write.
Login alerts from places or devices you do not know.
Your password no longer works, or the recovery email or phone number has changed.
Friends say they received strange links or money requests from you.

steps: Do not panic and do not pay anyone who offers to 'get it back'.
Use a device you trust to change the password to a new, unique one. If you cannot log in, use the service's 'forgot password' or account recovery.
Secure your email first, since it can reset everything else. Change its password and turn on two-step verification.
Sign out all other devices from the security settings and remove unknown devices or apps connected to the account.
Check recovery email, phone number and forwarding rules, and fix anything you did not set.
Change the password anywhere you reused the old one.
Warn friends and family that the account was hacked, using another channel, so they ignore any strange messages.
Report the hacked account to the service using its help or report option. If money was lost, tell your bank or provider and the police.

body.p: Worked example: Adaeze clicked a link in a message claiming her exam results were ready and typed her social media password on the page. An hour later her friends say she is asking for airtime money. She uses her laptop to reset her password, signs out other devices, turns on two-step verification, and posts a note on another channel telling friends to ignore the messages. She also changes the same password on her email, where she had reused it.

Hacks are not a reason for shame. Look at what happened: was the password reused, was there a fake link, was two-step verification off? Fix that gap. Keep a recent backup so that even a total loss of an account does not cost you important files.

body.tip: If you are asked to pay to recover an account, it is almost always another scam.

body.p: Online life is real life. Cyberbullying means using phones, social media, games or messaging to hurt, threaten, embarrass or exclude someone. It can include insults, spreading rumours, sharing private photos without permission, making fake accounts, or leaving someone out of a group on purpose. Because it can happen any time of day and be seen by many people, it can feel overwhelming.

steps: Do not reply in anger. It often makes things worse.
Save evidence: take screenshots with dates, names and links.
Block the person and use the platform's report option.
Tell a trusted adult or friend, such as a parent, teacher or school counsellor. You do not have to deal with it alone.

If you are threatened, or your private images are shared, tell an adult and, where needed, the police. In many countries sharing intimate images of a person under 18 is a serious crime, even if the person agreed to take them.

body.p: If it is affecting your sleep, studies or mood, speak to someone you trust or a local helpline or counsellor. Asking for help is a strength.

body.h: If you see it happen to someone else

list: Do not join in, laugh, or forward the content.
Support the person privately with a kind message.
Report the content and tell an adult.
If someone seems in danger of hurting themselves, tell a trusted adult or emergency services immediately.

body.p: Before posting, ask three questions: Is it true? Is it kind? Would I be comfortable if my teacher, parent or future employer saw it? Do not share someone's photo, voice note or private chat without their permission. Group chats feel private, but any member can copy and share what you write.

Worked example: Tendai notices a classmate's embarrassing photo is circulating in the class WhatsApp group. He does not forward it. He messages the classmate to say he is sorry it happened, screenshots the group evidence, and tells the class teacher, who helps get the group administrator to remove the photo and deal with those who started it.

body.tip: Report first, then block. Blocking alone can remove your ability to see what is being said.

quiz.q: Sandra uses the same password for her email, Facebook and her university portal. A small online shop she once joined announces a data leak. What is the best action?
options: Change each important password to a different strong one, starting with email, and turn on two-step verification
Change only the shop password, since that is the only site that leaked, and leave the other accounts as they are
Wait a few weeks to see whether anything strange happens before spending time changing any of your passwords
Add a new number to the end of your current password and keep using that slightly changed version on all three

quiz.q: Which password is the best choice for a main email account?
options: Your first name and birth year with an exclamation mark at the end
A four-word passphrase made of unrelated words, used nowhere else
The name of your favourite football club written in capital letters
An eight-character password that you also use for your school portal

quiz.q: You get an SMS: 'Your mobile-money account will be closed today. Reply with your PIN to keep it open.' What should you do?
options: Reply quickly with the PIN so the account is not closed and you can keep using your money today
Call the number given in the SMS to confirm that the message is genuine before you decide anything
Do not send the PIN, and check with the provider through its official number or app
Forward the message to friends to warn them, then send the PIN to be safe in case it is real

quiz.q: An online scholarship says you have won, but you must pay a processing fee before the funds are released. What is the most sensible response?
options: Pay the small fee because it is far cheaper than losing a large scholarship you have already won
Pay half of the fee now and the other half once the award letter arrives in your email inbox
Send your bank details so that the fee can be deducted directly from your winnings when paid
Treat it as a likely scam, do not pay, and verify it on the awarding organisation's official website

quiz.q: A recruiter on social media offers a well-paid data entry job but asks you to pay for a uniform and training before you start. What should you do?
options: Decline, because a real employer does not charge you to be hired, and report the profile
Pay the fee, because paying for training and a uniform is normal for well-paid office jobs
Pay only if the recruiter first sends you a photo of a staff ID card to prove the job is real
Ask a friend to pay the fee first as a test, and pay yourself only if the friend gets the job

quiz.q: You must check a bank balance while waiting at a bus station with free Wi-Fi and 2 GB of mobile data. What is the safest choice?
options: Use your mobile data connection instead of the public Wi-Fi
Use the free Wi-Fi, because it is faster and saves your data
Use the free Wi-Fi but type your password carefully and slowly
Ask the person selling at the stall to log in to the bank for you

quiz.q: A free photo-editing app asks for access to your contacts, microphone and location. What is the best response?
options: Allow everything, because apps need all the permissions they ask for to work properly on a phone
Deny permissions it does not need for editing, and reconsider the app if it refuses to work without them
Allow everything but only use the app while your phone is connected to a public Wi-Fi network
Allow everything and then give the app a five-star review to thank the developer for being free

quiz.q: Your phone suddenly shows no signal for hours, although friends nearby have signal. You then receive an email saying your number was changed to a new SIM. What should you do first?
options: Wait until tomorrow to see if the signal comes back before you contact anyone about the email
Restart the phone repeatedly and keep checking for signal, without contacting your provider or bank
Use another phone or Wi-Fi to contact your network provider and bank straight away to block the swap
Post on social media asking if anyone else has the same problem and wait for helpful replies

quiz.q: A caller says they are from your mobile-money provider and asks you to read out the code just sent to you so they can 'cancel a fraud'. What do you do?
options: Read the code to them, because they already know your full name and phone number
Read out half of the code and keep the other half to yourself, to be safe
Ask them to call back, and give the code at that point if they sound polite
Hang up, do not share the code, and call the provider on its official number

quiz.q: You receive money from a number you do not know, then a message: 'Sorry, wrong number, please send it back.' What is the best action?
options: Check the transaction in the official app or with the provider, and send nothing back until it confirms
Send the money back immediately to be polite, because it obviously reached you by mistake and the sender sounds upset
Keep the money and ignore the message without checking anything, since you never asked for it and it is now yours
Send half back to the sender and keep the other half as a fair reward for the trouble of sorting it out

quiz.q: Your social media account has been hacked and friends say it is asking them for airtime. What should you do first, from a device you trust?
options: Remove all your friends from the account straight away so that none of them can be targeted, then wait
Change to a new unique password, sign out other devices, turn on two-step verification and warn friends another way
Pay the person who says they can return the account a small fee, then change the password once it is back
Create a brand new account and abandon the hacked one without telling anyone, hoping the hacker will lose interest

quiz.q: After a hack you notice the account's recovery email was changed to an unknown address. Why is it important to fix this?
options: Because the attacker could use it to get back in or reset your password again
Because an unfamiliar address makes your profile look untidy to anyone who visits it
Because the extra recovery email uses up your mobile data every time the app syncs
Because your friends can see the address and may be confused about whose account it is

quiz.q: A classmate is being insulted in a class group chat and someone shares an embarrassing photo of them. What is the most helpful thing to do?
options: Forward it to the other class group so that more people can see it and judge what happened
Join in with a joke about the photo so that you are not the next person they target
Do not forward it, support your classmate privately, save evidence, and report it to a trusted adult
Do nothing and stay out of it, because messages in a class group chat are private

quiz.q: You are a victim of repeated cruel messages. Which step best helps you deal with it?
options: Reply with equally cruel messages to teach the sender a lesson and make them stop
Delete the messages immediately so nobody ever sees them and the sender gets no attention
Keep it secret from adults, because telling someone will only make the bullying worse
Take screenshots as evidence, block and report the sender, and tell a trusted adult

quiz.q: Your phone holds your final-year project, which exists only on that phone. What is the best way to protect it?
options: Rely on the phone's internal memory, because it is safe enough for a single project file
Keep a backup in a cloud account or on another device, and check that it works
Send the file to a friend's phone number once, then delete your own copy to save space
Make a second copy of the file on the same phone, in a different folder, and rely on it
